1060408: In a real debate you don't think in grammar lessons, but in what you need to do. To give and deny opinions: «creo que + indicative», «no creo que + subjunctive», «no es que… sino que…». ubafka: A presentation is easier to follow when the listener knows where they are. To order, use «en primer lugar… en segundo lugar… por último», «para empezar» or «a continuación»; to present two sides, «por un lado… por otro (lado)» or «por una parte… por otra». To add, «además» and «asimismo» (more formal); «es más» and «incluso» raise the strength of the argument; «encima» also adds, but it is colloquial and usually sounds like a complaint.
q7tpwu: To give examples, «por ejemplo», «es el caso de» or «pongamos por caso». To rephrase, «es decir», «o sea» (more spoken) and «en otras palabras»; «mejor dicho» corrects what you have just said: «son trescientos comercios, mejor dicho, doscientos ochenta». In writing, these connectors usually go between commas or after a semicolon.

ypwgc9: To draw consequences, «por (lo) tanto», «por consiguiente» and «así que»; «de ahí que» takes the subjunctive: «el tránsito se duplicó; de ahí que los vecinos pidan cambios». To close, «en resumen», «en definitiva» or «en conclusión»; «total, que…» is colloquial. To refute, remember the mood: «no es cierto que + subjunctive» denies, and «es cierto que + indicative» concedes before objecting. «Al contrario» comes after a negated idea; «no…, sino (más bien)…» replaces one idea with another; «lejos de + infinitive» presents the opposite of what was expected; «en absoluto» is a flat «no»; «nada más lejos de la realidad» denies emphatically.
u79k85: To attribute an idea to someone else, «según + noun» (or «según tú»), «de acuerdo con» and «como señala…». Attributing well is part of refuting well: first you state fairly what the other person thinks and then you argue against it.

rsrlfr: Original SpanishCue text written as an opinion column in a fictional Almagro newspaper in Buenos Aires. The people, the figures and the report are invented.
watoy: Few proposals have divided the neighbourhood as much as the one to pedestrianise the market street at weekends. Since the residents' association presented it in March, meetings fill up, messaging groups are ablaze and, at the market entrance, there's more arguing than shopping. This column doesn't aim to close the debate, but to put it in order: to separate what we know from what we suppose and to answer the arguments that circulate most.
j57147: Firstly, it's worth remembering where the idea comes from. The association has been calling since 2019 for a solution for the pavements, whose width in some stretches is no more than a metre and a half. On Saturday mornings, when the market is full, walking with a pushchair is almost impossible. Consequently, the problem exists and nobody has invented it. What is being discussed is the solution, and on that it's worth listening to everyone who lives and works on the block, not only to those who shout loudest at meetings.
1lj0b6q: The most repeated argument against it is that the pedestrian street would empty the neighbourhood. According to the shopkeepers who hold this view, customers would stop coming if they can't park. It is not true, however, that most of them arrive by car. The study carried out by the Universidad del Oeste last year, and not the one commissioned by the council, shows that almost half of customers arrive on foot and only one in five comes by car. It is true that this fifth spends more, which is why shops selling materials, such as Ricardo Benítez's hardware shop, have reason to be worried.
60a2pu: The second argument holds that the proposal is improvised. Nothing could be further from the truth: the text the association presented is twenty pages long, includes a loading and unloading schedule from six to ten in the morning and provides for exceptions for residents with reduced mobility. That said, a good document is no substitute for a consultation. If the council had asked the shopkeepers from the start, there wouldn't be so much distrust today, and many of them wouldn't have found out about the proposal from the papers.
sn2jwa: Far from being a dead end, the debate has produced a reasonable idea: a six-month trial, with measurements of sales, traffic and noise, and a binding consultation at the end. By March, as the councillor for mobility has announced, the traffic study will have been published, so the trial could begin in autumn. There must also be intermediate formulas: closing only on Sundays, for example, or providing a loading area for shops that sell heavy goods.
1j1agfz: In short, the pedestrian street is neither the panacea some imagine nor the disaster others predict. It is a tool, and as such it must be measured. Of the residents who support it we ask patience; of the shopkeepers who fear it, that they agree to look at the data. And the council, we would be grateful if, for once, it did not decide behind closed doors what will be lived in full view of everyone.
